body: The brake cable has been slipping for a fortnight. Ten past nine on a Tuesday night, and a man is kneeling on the concrete floor of a garage with a child’s bicycle upside down in front of him. He gets the tension wrong, backs the nut off, gets it wrong the other way, and sits back on his heels with cold hands and a torch held in his teeth. The boy it belongs to went up to bed an hour ago and does not know the bicycle is in here. In the morning it will simply work, and nothing will be said about it.

Nobody watched that. Nobody will hear about it. The boy will ride to school on Wednesday with a brake that bites properly and will never once think about the man on the concrete floor, and that is not a failure of gratitude on his part. That is the shape of the job.

Like arrows in the hand of a warrior, so are the children of one’s youth. The line gets quoted warmly, usually across a table with a full house around it, and the warmth skips straight past the part of the image that is doing all of the work.

It is worth taking the word arrow literally for a moment rather than admiring it as a figure of speech. An arrow is a made thing and a slow one to make. The shaft has to be straight, and it has to be the right stiffness for the bow it will be shot from, and no amount of goodwill substitutes for either. The fletching goes on last, and it is the part that keeps the flight honest once the hand is out of it. Then the whole object is loosed. Everything about its construction assumes a moment when the maker stops being able to influence it, and every fault built in early shows up at the far end, at distance, where it can no longer be reached.

This band has a frequency set aside for the subject. HM 385.50 — Raising Arrows — is assigned and in build, not yet on air, still silent. The dial itself runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, of which 46 are playing at this moment.

Raising for release costs more than raising for company, and almost none of the difference is visible while it is being paid. It means teaching a child to do without you on purpose, at the exact age when being needed is the pleasant part. It means letting a decision stand that you could have overruled, and then living with a fortnight of the consequences in your own house. An arrow is not for keeping. The entire purpose of the work is that the thing leaves your hand, and a parent who cannot say that out loud will quietly begin aiming for a shorter flight.

That has become a strange thing to say. The culture around raising children now runs on visible return: the photograph of the milestone, the small performance of a family that is going well. None of it is malicious and most of it is affectionate. But it trains a parent to want results on a timetable that can be shown to other people, and the work that actually sets a child’s aim is almost entirely unshowable. It happens on a Tuesday night on a concrete floor. It produces nothing to post and nothing to say.

Look at how a household actually teaches and it is not by conversations. It is by repetition, and by what is left running in the room — the hour the meal happens, the words said before it, the music that is on while nobody is listening to it. A child takes in the ordinary furniture of a house long before anybody sits them down to explain anything. The aim is set by ten thousand unremarkable hours rather than by three good talks, which is why the good talks so often land on a child who has already decided.
There is a rival account of what a family is for, and it is not a stupid one. It deserves to be taken at its strongest.

That account says the point of raising children well is that they stay close: a table that fills up at Christmas, grandchildren in the next street, a house everybody comes back to. Something in it is true. Families that scatter lose things that are hard to rebuild, and nearness does work that affection at a distance cannot. But it makes the parent the destination, and it quietly measures the work by proximity — which is the one measure the metaphor refuses. A quiver still full at the end of the battle is not a full quiver. It is an unused one.
An arrow is not for keeping.

A woman of about seventy is standing at the back of a village hall on a Saturday afternoon holding a paper cup of tea she has not drunk. There is a birthday going on and too many children in the room. Her grandson, who is six and has just been told to sit down, is singing something under his breath while he picks the icing off his plate. It takes her a few seconds to place it, because he has half the words wrong and the tune is going somewhere it should not. It is a chorus she used to sing on the school run, twenty-odd years ago, in a car with a broken heater, to a boy who is now in the corner of this hall arguing about a folding table. She does not mention it to anybody, then or afterwards.

Nobody in that hall taught that boy anything. The aim was set in a cold car two decades earlier by a woman who had no way of knowing and no way of checking, and the result surfaced at a distance, second hand, at a birthday party she nearly did not attend.

None of this comes with a guarantee, and the metaphor cuts in that direction too. Arrows go wide. Children raised with enormous care walk away from every part of it, and parents who did the years properly sit in quiet houses with phones that do not ring. Anybody selling a method that prevents this is selling something. The work is real and the outcome is genuinely not in the hand that did the work.

That is not a defect in the arrangement. It is the arrangement. A result you could guarantee would not be a person; it would be a project with a person-shaped output, and the thing you had raised would be incapable of the one act that makes any of it worth having, which is choosing it for themselves. Release is not a parenting technique to be mastered at eighteen. It is an admission of a limit that was there the whole time, and admitting it early is what stops the last few years turning into a grip.

So the job is aim, not hold. The years of drawing the bow are the ones nobody sees and nobody thanks you for — the brake cable, the same instruction for the ninth time, the hour kept when it would have been easier to let it go. The release is not the sad end of that work. It is the work, arriving. And the consolation on offer is thin and completely real: you will not get to watch most of it, and you will hear about the best of it second hand, years late, from somebody else.
All of which is theory until there is a house with children in it and a Wednesday morning to get through. So here is the part that is not theory.

The dial carries four kinds of programming and it is worth knowing they are there. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, gospel, hymns and country. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe: entertaining, clean, and playable in a room with children in it whether or not every track names God out loud. And there are the international stations, hosted in their own languages for the nations rather than translated into them afterwards. Four kinds, one dial, and no menu to work through to reach them.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 361.90 — Jubilee Kids Party. It is the station on this dial that does the part of the job this article has been describing, which is not the talk and not the milestone but the ordinary furniture of a house. It is loud and cheerful, made for breakfast and the back of a car, and it puts words into children while they are busy doing something else and not being taught anything. That is precisely how words get in. A child who is sung at for a few years ends up with a supply of lines nobody told them they were storing, and those are the lines that come back at a bus stop, or a village hall, or a hospital corridor, long after the person who put them there has stopped being able to help.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone is nearest, press play, and it plays — it is deliberately built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you want it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are really reaching for, which is how the next station gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than an offer. Put HM 361.90 on tomorrow morning while the toast is burning and a shoe is missing, and then leave it alone and get on with the morning. You will not see what it does. Neither did the man on the garage floor, and neither did the woman with the paper cup of tea, and both of them had already done the only part of it that was ever theirs to do.
